The morning light hit the windowsill differently that Tuesday, slanting through dust motes that had been undisturbed for years. Margaret watched them swirl like tiny galaxies in the amber glow and thought about her brother's hands, the way they'd trembled the last time she'd seen him, holding a coffee cup in a hospital cafeteria that smelled of industrial cleaner and lost causes.

She had not gone back to that hospital. She had not gone back to that city. She had, in fact, done her level best to not go back to anything at all, constructing a life of careful forward motion, each day a plank laid over an abyss she refused to look down into.

The dust motes settled. The light shifted. Somewhere in the apartment building, a neighbor's dog barked three times, paused, barked once more—a code Margaret had never learned to decipher.

She was fifty-three years old and had just discovered, while cleaning out a closet she'd avoided for six years, that her mother had kept every postcard Margaret had ever sent. The ones from college, terse and dutiful. The ones from her first marriage's dissolution, strangely euphoric in their brevity. The ones from the road trip after the diagnosis, when she'd driven through fourteen states in eleven days, sleeping in the car, writing lies about roadside attractions and local color while the radio played songs she couldn't stand.

The postcards filled a shoebox. Her mother's handwriting appeared on none of them. Margaret had never sent a return address. The correspondence had been one-way as a dropped call, and yet here was evidence that someone had been listening, had kept the line open, waiting for the next fragment to arrive.

She thought about calling her brother. The number she had was four years old. She thought about the tremor in his hands, whether it was the medication or the disease or simply the accumulated weight of being the one who stayed, who sat by the bed, who made the arrangements while Margaret drove through Nebraska cornfields and wrote about the world's largest ball of twine.

The dog barked again. The dust motes, disturbed by her movement through the room, resumed their slow procession through the light.

There was a theory Margaret had read somewhere, that every person who ever existed was still here, their atoms scattered and recombined into new configurations, so that each breath contained molecules once breathed by Caesar, by Woolf, by some anonymous child in a century no one remembered. She found this comforting and terrible in equal measure. The permanence without the person. The persistence without the purpose.

She made coffee she didn't want. She stood at the window and watched a man below struggle with a recalcitrant umbrella, the wind turning it inside out, then right side out, then inside out again, a mechanical meditation on the futility of shelter. She wanted to call down to him, to offer some wisdom she'd never earned, but the window was sealed, the glass old and thick with the accumulated residue of decades of rain and city grime and the strange, inert breath of all the previous tenants who had stood here just so, watching strangers wrestle with weather.

The postcards sat on the kitchen table. She had arranged them chronologically without deciding to, a narrative emerging from her hands rather than her will. Here was the trajectory of a life she barely recognized as her own: the eager student, the disappointed wife, the frightened daughter, the fleeing woman, the—what? The current iteration, standing in borrowed light, uncertain what came next.

Her phone buzzed. A number she didn't recognize. She let it go to voicemail, then immediately listened. A creditor, a wrong number, a voice from the past she'd failed to identify in the three seconds of message before the hang-up. She played it again. The voice said only "Margaret," then stopped, as if the name itself were the entire message, sufficient and complete.

She did not call back. She did not know how.

The coffee went cold. The man with the umbrella had surrendered it to the wind, and she watched it cartwheel down the street, a black flower tumbling through the gray afternoon, briefly beautiful in its uselessness, its refusal to be what it was made for.

She thought about her mother's hands, which had also trembled, near the end. The way they'd plucked at the blanket, at the air, at some invisible thread only she could see. Margaret had not been there for that, either. She had been in a motel in Arizona, writing a postcard she never sent, about a meteor crater that had struck her as obscene in its scale, its indifference to what it had obliterated.

The shoebox had other things in it. A photograph of her parents before she was born, her father holding a fish with the embarrassed pride of a man who had never learned to display emotion directly. A lock of hair, blonde turning brown, presumably hers. A ticket stub from a concert she didn't remember attending, the band name unfamiliar, the date falling in a year she associated with nothing but waiting, with the suspended animation of a life deferred.

She had 1000 words, or the promise of them. She had this room, this light, this particular arrangement of dust and silence and the faint hum of a refrigerator she kept meaning to replace. She had a brother who might be dead by now, for all she knew. She had a mother who had kept her postcards without ever once, in all the years, mentioning that she had received them, that they mattered, that the daughter who wrote them mattered, existed, was real and present and desperate for some sign that her transmissions were not simply vanishing into the void.

The wind shifted. The light changed. The dust motes found new patterns, new temporary geometries in the air.

Margaret sat at the table. She picked up a pen she couldn't remember buying. She wrote, on the back of the oldest postcard, the one from her freshman dormitory with its optimistic lie about making friends, the words: *I am here. I have always been here. I did not know you knew.*

She did not know who to send it to. She addressed it to herself, at this address, in this room, in this particular slant of afternoon light that would never come again in exactly this configuration, with exactly these dust motes, exactly this silence pressing against the windows like something trying to get in, or out, or through.

The pen ran dry. The postcard remained unfinished. She placed it on top of the others, a new beginning or a final end, she couldn't tell which, didn't need to know, had stopped needing to know anything except that she was here, that the light kept changing, that someone, once, had kept her words without telling her, had held them in the dark, had waited.

The dog barked. The refrigerator hummed. The wind, outside, did whatever wind does when no one is watching, when no one has an umbrella to lose, when the world continues in its ordinary, unbearable, sufficient way, without waiting for permission, without requiring witness, simply here, simply now, simply enough.
